candidates.headline: A word-level co-occurrence correlation does not imply that position-level heavy hitters arise from co-occurrence
candidates.claim: The paper explains heavy hitters by co-occurrence, using an analysis per vocabulary word type. The deployed policy keeps token positions within one sequence, per head. The paper's own appendix names two other possible sources of high accumulated score: the bias from accumulating past scores and a concentration at sentence beginnings. The origin of the heavy-hitter regularity is therefore not established for the unit that is actually evicted.
candidates.paper_fact: Additionally, we can see the accumulated attention score of each word (in red dots) have a high correlation with their co-occurrences in the data (gray curve).
candidates.premise: Aggregating attention by word type over a corpus averages out position effects. Under causal masking, early positions are attended by more later queries, so they accumulate more mass regardless of word identity. Sink-like behavior at sequence start also concentrates attention independently of co-occurrence.
candidates.inference: The word-level correlation (Fig 2b, with the x-axis being the word index in the vocabulary) does not show that the positions selected by H2O are the ones selected because of co-occurrence. Part of the heavy-hitter signal may come from position-driven accumulation and start-of-sentence effects. In that case the regularity would shift with prompt style or model family in ways the co-occurrence story does not predict.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement. In a 100-token sequence, token 1 is attended by 100 queries and token 90 by 10. Even if both have equal per-query attention, token 1 has 10 times the accumulated mass. A word-type aggregate would not reveal this.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If position accumulation or sink behavior drives much of the signal, then H2 selection tracks token age and start-of-text rather than importance. Behavior would change when prompt formats move the informative content away from the start or from frequent words.
candidates.critical_link: The word-type-level correlation is used to explain the position-level, per-head eviction set.
necessary_conditions: Position accumulation or sink effects contribute materially to accumulated score
The evaluated workloads do not separate these effects from co-occurrence
defeaters: Per-position scores within a sequence also correlate with word frequency
Ablations show removing H2 hurts accuracy (Fig 2c), which supports their importance regardless of origin
The averaged-score variant, tried to counter the bias, degraded performance, so any bias may be benign
do_not_infer: Do not infer that H2 tokens are unimportant
Do not infer that co-occurrence plays no role
Do not infer that H2O accuracy results are wrong

candidates.headline: A '20% KV cache budget' does not imply a 5x memory reduction when the implementation keeps K heavy hitters plus K recent tokens
candidates.claim: The headline '5x reduction' holds only if the reported percentage is the total retained fraction (K/2 per half). The appendix describes a cache of 2K entries built from K per half, and the paper never states which reading the percentage follows. If the percentage is the per-half K, the real retained fraction is about 40% and the reduction about 2.5x.
candidates.paper_fact: we always maintain a list of KV cache with the first K entries as heavy hitters, and the last K entries as most recent tokens.
candidates.premise: A cache that holds K heavy-hitter entries plus K recent entries holds 2K entries per head. Memory reduction is the ratio of full-prompt length to retained entries.
candidates.inference: The paper calls the budget '20% of the prompt's length' and then reports more than 5x reduction. The appendix parameterises the cache by K per half. If '20%' means K/prompt_length, the retained fraction is 2K/prompt_length = 40%, so the reduction is 2.5x, not 5x. The text does not settle which definition the experiments used. The sizes in Figure 9 are given in absolute tokens, which does not settle it either.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: prompt length 1000. If K = 200 per half, 400 entries are kept (40%, 2.5x reduction). If the total is 200 (K = 100 per half), the figure is 20% (5x reduction).
candidates.conditional_consequence: If '20%' denotes K per half, then every 'up to 5x memory reduction' and every '20% budget' comparison against baselines such as Local or Sparse Transformer (budget-matched) overstates compression by about 2x. Throughput gains from larger batch sizes would then rest on a smaller memory saving than claimed.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the percentage in the experiments is the total cache fraction or the per-half K. The paper does not state this.
necessary_conditions: The experiment code passes the percentage as K, not as 2K, to the selection routine.
Baselines (Local, Sparse Transformer) are budgeted by the same percentage figure, not by the number of entries retained.
defeaters: Experiments convert the percentage to total entries and split it in half, so K = 10% each.
The 'more than 5x' statement is derived from measured memory usage, not from the nominal percentage.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the reported accuracies are wrong.
Do not infer that H2O fails to reduce memory.
Do not infer that the throughput numbers are wrong, since they may be measured with actual cache sizes.

candidates.headline: Per-step attention sparsity above 95% does not imply that a persistent 5% KV cache (a 20x reduction) is sufficient
candidates.claim: The paper measures sparsity separately for each softmax row, but H2O evicts permanently. The 5% / 20x argument therefore compares a per-step quantity with a persistent-set quantity. The reduction that holds across all steps depends on how stable the important positions are over time, and the paper does not measure that stability in this observation.
candidates.paper_fact: Therefore, only 5% of the KV cache is sufficient for decoding the same output token at each generation step, which suggests it may be possible to have up to a 20× reduction in KV cache size without an accuracy drop.
candidates.premise: A cache that never re-admits evicted entries must cover the union of the positions needed over all future steps. That union is at least as large as the support at any single step, and it grows if the support drifts across steps or heads.
candidates.inference: If the per-row sparse supports differ across decoding steps, the persistent cache needed to avoid accuracy loss exceeds the per-step 5%. The 20x figure is then an upper bound on potential savings, not an expectation. The paper's later results use a 20% budget, which is consistent with this reading but does not establish its cause.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement. Suppose each step needs only 5 of 100 positions, but a different set of 5 each time. Over 20 steps the union is all 100 positions, so a permanent 5-slot cache would miss most future needs.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the important positions drift across steps, a permanent cache must be much larger than 5% to avoid misses. The realized reduction would then be well below 20x.
candidates.critical_link: Per-step row sparsity is treated as if it set the size of a persistent set of retained positions, with no measurement of how much supports overlap across steps.
necessary_conditions: Important positions at step t differ at least partly from those at step t+1.
Eviction is irreversible, as in the H2O policy.
Accuracy depends on attention mass from positions outside the retained set.
defeaters: Supports are highly stable across steps and heads, so the union stays near 5%.
Heavy-hitter accumulation plus the recent window captures the drifting positions well.
The authors present 5% only as motivation ('suggests it may be possible'), not as a guarantee.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the observation is false.
Do not infer that 20% is the minimum safe budget.
Do not infer that support drift is the sole reason the paper's experiments use a 20% budget.
candidates.lens: L3/L1 unit mismatch and proxy guarantee: per-step row sparsity versus a persistent retained set

candidates.headline: A visual correlation with word co-occurrence does not imply that word frequency explains heavy hitters
candidates.claim: The paper presents the link between accumulated attention and co-occurrence as a 'high correlation' read from a plot. It gives no coefficient, and the appendix reports a position effect (heavy hitters at sentence starts) that frequency alone does not obviously explain. The origin of heavy hitters is therefore not established.
candidates.paper_fact: Additionally, we can see the accumulated attention score of each word (in red dots) have a high correlation with their co-occurrences in the data (gray curve).
candidates.premise: Frequent tokens, such as function words, punctuation, and sentence starts, also tend to sit at structurally privileged positions. Attention-sink effects can concentrate mass on early or delimiter tokens regardless of word identity.
candidates.inference: Correlation with frequency is compatible with both a word-frequency account and a position or attention-sink account. The paper's own observation about sentence-initial H2s indicates a position component, so the abstract's 'natural' emergence from co-occurrence is under-identified.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: a rare token placed at the start of every sentence might still receive a large accumulated score. A frequent token in mid-sentence might not.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If position or sink effects dominate, then inputs with unusual structure or many rare tokens could show a different heavy-hitter set than word frequency predicts, and a frequency-based explanation would not transfer.
candidates.critical_link: Whether frequency, position, or both drive accumulated attention is not tested.
necessary_conditions: Position and frequency must be separable in the data, for example by shuffling or controlled inputs.
defeaters: The correlation may be genuinely strong even without a coefficient.
Frequency and sentence-start effects may be mutually consistent, since sentence-initial words are often frequent.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the correlation is absent or weak.
Do not infer that the H2O algorithm depends on the frequency explanation, since it uses online accumulated scores.

the emergence of H2 is natural and strongly correlates with the frequent co-occurrence of tokens in the text

candidates.headline: The 'mild assumptions' label does not imply the per-step universal conditions are mild, since their tolerances scale as 1/n
candidates.claim: The abstract says the guarantee holds under mild assumptions. The formal proof invokes universal monotone, dynamic and approximation conditions for every step i, with tolerances θ=γ=α/(10n) and ε0=β/(10n). Those conditions must hold at ever-tighter tolerance as sequence length n grows. Their validity for real attention is not tested in the paper.
candidates.paper_fact: The proof follows from using Theorem D.17, Corollary D.18, Lemma D.30 with choosing ϵ0 = β/(10n) and θ = γ = α/(10n).
candidates.premise: A guarantee obtained by chaining n inductive steps, each losing a factor (1-θ)(1-γ) or an additive ε0, stays meaningful only if each per-step loss is O(1/n). A universal condition must therefore hold with slack O(1/n) at every token.
candidates.inference: Lemma D.30 loses an additive ε0 per step, giving (i+1)·ε0, and a factor (1-θ) per step, giving (1-θ)^{i+1}. To keep the total loss at β and α, the paper sets ε0, θ, γ to 1/(10n) of the target. Definitions D.25/D.26 and D.28 then require, for every i and every admissible S_i, that fS_i,i(S_i) ≥ (1-θ)·fS_{i-1},i-1(S_i) and opt_i ≥ (1-γ)·opt_{i-1}. These are quantitative regularity requirements on the attention surrogate across steps. Submodularity is motivated by a coverage analogy (D.7), not verified on attention.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement. If n=4000 and α=0.1, then θ=γ=0.1/40000=2.5e-6. Each step's value must change by less than that relative amount, and the approximate score must be within β/40000 of the exact one.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the real attention surrogate violates the dynamic conditions at even a few steps by more than 1/(10n), the stated bound no longer follows from the proof. The mildness of the assumptions would then not be established for long sequences.
candidates.critical_link: Whether real attention satisfies the universal dynamic, monotone and approximation conditions at tolerance proportional to 1/n at every step.
necessary_conditions: The theorem's constants are chosen exactly as in Theorem D.32's proof.
The conditions are required for all i and all admissible sets, as stated in Definitions D.25/D.26/D.28.
defeaters: The conditions might hold with margin in practice for attention, given how smoothly attention scores change per step.
A tighter analysis might remove the 1/n dependence.
do_not_infer: Do not infer the conditions are violated; the paper neither tests nor refutes them.
Do not infer the algorithm degrades with length; the paper reports streaming up to four million tokens empirically, which is separate from the theorem.

candidates.headline: Removing eviction data movement does not guarantee throughput keeps scaling once memory is freed
candidates.claim: No-swap in-place replacement cuts I/O on eviction and lets batches grow. This does not ensure throughput scales with the freed memory, because the bottleneck can shift to compute or dequantization.
candidates.paper_fact: Despite the batch size being enlarged by 20 times, the actual throughput improvement is less than 2 times.
candidates.premise: In offloaded inference the PCIe transfer is often the bottleneck. When the cache fits on the GPU, per-step compute, quantization and score upkeep become the limiting terms.
candidates.inference: The paper's own quantized-H2O result shows throughput growing far less than batch size. By the same pattern, the I/O savings from the no-swap design should give diminishing returns once PCIe stops being the bottleneck. The paper attributes the sub-linear scaling to inefficient quantization, not to the no-swap mechanism, so the extension is inferred.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: if I/O were 70% of step time and the no-swap design removed all of it, the step time would fall to 30% and the speedup would cap near 3.3x however large the batch grows.
candidates.conditional_consequence: On hardware or configurations where the KV cache already fits on the GPU, the benefit of in-place replacement over FlexGen is smaller than in the offloaded T4 settings.
candidates.critical_link: The gain is tied to PCIe I/O being the dominant cost, which holds in the CPU-offload T4 tests.

Compute or dequantization overhead is comparable to I/O

candidates.headline: Accumulated-score eviction does not guarantee that H2O's advantage over a static sink persists as the stream grows
candidates.claim: In H2O, token scores are running sums of attention with no decay or normalization by age. Over a very long stream, the retained heavy-hitter set can therefore be dominated by early, long-accumulating tokens. It would then behave like a near-static prefix, which is what StreamingLLM keeps by rule, and H2O's edge over StreamingLLM could shrink with stream length.
candidates.paper_fact: In H2O, employing the accumulated attention score to evict KV embeddings can lead to a potential bias favoring the least recent tokens.
candidates.premise: A sum of nonnegative per-step attention weights grows with the number of steps a token has been observed. Softmax rows sum to 1, so total score mass grows linearly with time. A token that has been present for millions of steps can hold a much larger sum than one that has been present for hundreds.
candidates.inference: Without decay, a late-arriving token that matters only briefly cannot overtake long-resident early tokens, so the heavy-hitter slots can freeze on early content. The paper reports the bias but does not test it at multi-million-token scale. It also tried averaged scores only on benchmarks, where they degraded performance.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: an early token receives 0.05 attention per step. After 1,000,000 steps its score is 50,000. A new token receiving 0.3 attention per step for 1,000 steps reaches 300 and is evicted first.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If scores are never decayed or rescaled, H2O's perplexity gap over StreamingLLM would be expected to narrow or vanish as the stream grows. The retained set would converge to a fixed early-token set plus the local window.
candidates.critical_link: Scores accumulated over unbounded time dominate comparisons against recently admitted tokens.
necessary_conditions: Scores accumulate without decay in the long-stream setting.
The heavy-hitter budget is small relative to the number of early high-attention tokens.
The local window does not hold the tokens needed later.
defeaters: The implementation resets or rescales scores periodically.
Early tokens' attention falls off enough that their sums stop dominating.
Figure 5 shows a persistent gap to four million tokens, which would then be explained by something other than adaptive selection.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that H2O is worse than StreamingLLM at any length.
Do not infer that the authors' four-million-token result is wrong.
Do not infer that accumulated scores always freeze the retained set.

candidates.headline: Recognizing the accumulated-score age bias does not imply that averaging the score removes it or improves eviction
candidates.claim: The authors identify that summing attention over queries favors older tokens, but their own fix (averaging) degraded performance. So the age bias of the sum is not shown to be a defect to remove. It may partly act as useful retention of early, sink-like tokens, and the paper does not test that.
candidates.paper_fact: employing the accumulated attention score to evict KV embeddings can lead to a potential bias favoring the least recent tokens.
candidates.premise: In a causally masked decoder, a token at position j is attended to by every later query, so a sum over queries grows with token age. A mean divides out the number of queries and removes that exposure effect. Early tokens such as the first tokens of a sequence often receive disproportionately large attention in autoregressive LMs.
candidates.inference: If the mean is the fairer importance estimate yet performs worse, the sum's age-proportional term may be correlated with what the model needs, for example initial tokens that the authors say play a substantial role. The sum may therefore be doing implicit sink retention in addition to counting importance. The paper does not separate these two effects.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement. Two tokens each receive attention 0.1 from every query that sees them. Token A is at position 1 and token B at position n-4, with n=100. Sum scores: A=10.0, B=0.5. Mean scores: both 0.1. The sum keeps A, and the mean cannot distinguish them, so a tie-break rule would decide which is evicted.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If early tokens act as attention sinks, replacing the sum with a mean (or any age-normalized score) without explicitly pinning the first tokens could evict sinks and reduce quality. This is what the reported degradation would be consistent with.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the quality loss from averaging comes from evicting sink-like early tokens or from noisy averages of recently added tokens. The paper does not test either.
necessary_conditions: The averaged variant is implemented per-head with the same recent/heavy-hitter split as the summed variant.
Early tokens carry importance that the mean fails to register.
The degradation is not due to a noisy mean on tokens seen by few queries.
defeaters: A mean with a minimum-observation prior could outperform the sum.
The degradation may come from implementation details or hyperparameters of the averaged run.
Pinning the first tokens could remove the need for age bias.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the sum is optimal.
Do not infer that sink retention is the confirmed cause of the degradation.
Do not infer that the age bias is harmless at all context lengths.

candidates.headline: Reduced repetition under H2O eviction does not imply or guarantee better text modeling; it may be a side effect of lost context
candidates.claim: The paper presents lower Self-BELU and less repetition as a 'bonus' of H2O. Its own framing is that evicted KV entries are never seen again. A plausible alternative cause is that eviction removes the earlier tokens a repeating phrase would copy from. In that case the diversity gain is an information-loss side effect, and no faithfulness or recall metric accompanies it.
candidates.paper_fact: Since the evicted KV will not be seen in the future steps, dropping certain critical KV embeddings can cause a severe functional collapse, resulting in significant performance degradation
candidates.premise: Loops such as 'so moved that ... so moved that' typically rely on attention to earlier occurrences of the repeated phrase (induction-style copying). If eviction drops those earlier tokens, the copy loop can break regardless of whether the model is otherwise better.
candidates.inference: Under the paper's own description of eviction, the reduction in repetition is consistent with discarded context rather than improved generation. The paper reports no faithfulness metric on the same outputs to separate the two causes. The paper does not claim a mechanism, so this is an inferred alternative, not a reported finding.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: an output that avoids repeating 'the musician began to cry' because that earlier sentence was evicted would look more diverse. It might also fail to remember that a musician was mentioned, which a recall-based task would reveal.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the diversity comes from eviction removing the repeated context, a faithfulness or recall-sensitive evaluation on the same generations would show degradation, or no gain, alongside the lower Self-BELU. The diversity claim would then not reflect a quality improvement.
candidates.critical_link: Attributing reduced repetition to H2O's heavy-hitter selection without ruling out that dropped context, rather than better modeling, removes the repetition.
necessary_conditions: The repeated phrases in the full-model outputs depend on attention to evicted earlier tokens
Decoding uses a setting where repetition loops occur, such as greedy or low-temperature decoding
defeaters: Repetition rates still differ under sampling-based decoding, indicating the effect does not depend on loop avoidance

Do not infer that the diversity effect is absent; only its cause and meaning are unclear
Do not infer that the effect disappears under sampling; this is not tested

candidates.headline: Accumulated attention score does not imply token importance at prefill
candidates.claim: Prefill selects heavy hitters by summing attention over the prompt. Under a causal mask, earlier tokens are attended to by more queries and accumulate larger sums. The selection can therefore favor early positions independent of importance, and the paper's own alternative (averaging) did worse.
candidates.paper_fact: In H2O, employing the accumulated attention score to evict KV embeddings can lead to a potential bias favoring the least recent tokens.
candidates.premise: In causal attention, key j receives probability mass from the n−j+1 queries at or after position j. Each row sums to 1, so earlier keys appear in more rows. Unnormalized column sums are therefore position-biased.
candidates.inference: One-shot prefill selection ranks prompt tokens partly by position, which can inflate early tokens.
